title: Token shelf-life and granularity lab
content:
Context and goal:
- Personal scratchpad to explore a different credit model: credits with variable shelf-life + finer granularity units than 'token' or 'session'.
- Aim: reduce gaming, align subsidies with latency-sensitive workloads, and smooth revenue recognition for pay-as-you-go and committed customers.

Core ideas (high level):
1) Two-tier credit currency: ephemeral credits (E) and persistent credits (P)
   - E credits: meant for short-lived interactive work (chat, explorations). Expires after N days of inactivity (shelf-life). Cheap to issue as promos.
   - P credits: long-lived, purchased/committed currency for predictable workloads (batch embeddings, nightly jobs). No expiry or long shelf-life (~365d).
   - Rationale: preserves incentives to onboard and prevents long-term erosion of committed revenue by unlimited promo stacking.

2) Granularity buckets: micro-units that bridge tokens and sessions
   - micro-token (mt): ~16-32 tokens grain used to price tiny in-UI completions, reduces rounding waste for short answers.
   - response-unit (ru): amortizes outgoing costs per response header (latency/overhead). Useful for very short replies that otherwise look cheap by token but expensive due to latency.
   - gpu-minute-credit (gmc): tracks heavy offline/batched compute usage (align with Dedicated commits).

3) Shelf-life heuristics (configurable per-campaign):
   - promo E credits: expire 14 days after last use (encourages activation).
   - trial E credits: expire 60 days.
   - referral E credits: expire 90 days.
   - conversion to P credits permitted at a discount within X days of issuance (capture retailers).

Back-of-envelope unit math (very rough):
Assumptions:
- GPU cost for hosting baseline open model: $2.8 / GPU-hour (amortized infra + electricity + infra overhead for batch-oriented).
- Typical throughput for gen LM at median length: ~500 tokens/sec per GPU when fully utilized (varies wildly).
- Average token payload per interactive response: 80 tokens (user+assistant).
- Overhead per request (latency-specific cost): equivalent to 0.5 tokens due to routing/tracing/IO.

Compute => per-token cost: (2.8 $/hr) / (500 tokens/sec * 3600 sec/hr) = 2.8 / 1.8M ≈ $0.00000156 per token ~ 1.56e-6 USD/token.
Add infra overhead + inference stack margin (2–3x) => unit cost ≈ 4.5e-6 USD/token. Round to 5e-6 for safety.

Pricing sketches (tie to our credit units):
- micro-token (mt) = 16 tokens priced at 16 * 5e-6 = $0.00008 cost; list price 4x markup => $0.00032 per mt.
- response-unit (ru) = baseline 80 tokens + overhead => cost ~80 * 5e-6 + ru overhead = $0.0004 + $0.00005 => $0.00045; list price 3x => $0.00135 per ru.
- Burst/latency premium (for <50ms SLO) => surcharge 30% on ru price.
- gmc (gpu-minute-credit): 1 gmc = 1 GPU-minute; cost = $2.8 / 60 ≈ $0.0467; list price per gmc for Dedicated customers (committed) = $0.03 (we'd sell commits by bulk at discount), for payg-hosted = $0.06.

Scenario: Free trial flow design using shelf-life:
- Issue 1000 mt as trial E credits (equiv ~16k tokens). Expire in 14d.
- Provide 10 free ru (for API responses testing) expiring 7d.
- Incentivize conversion: if user purchases a monthly starter pack within 21d, 50% of remaining E->P transferable.

Anti-gaming and edge cases:
- Detect automated farming of short replies: monitor ru:qps per account > 2000 ru/day -> throttle and mark credits as audit-pending.
- Allow customer to burn E credits as 'one-time tip' for longer shelf-life conversion, at a small fee (prevents perpetual free stockpiling).
- Refund mechanics: P credits refundable only via account credits balance with 30d hold.

Metrics to track (dashboard); minimum viable signals:
- E->P conversion rate within 30d; goal > 8% for trial cohorts.
- Average credits consumed per active user per week (split E vs P).
- Unused E credits aging distribution (0-7d, 8-30d, 31-90d).
- RU churn: RU-heavy accounts that consume >70% RU relative to mt (indicative of low token but high overhead -> possible price mismatch).

Open questions / decisions to make:
- How to present units in the UI without confusing developers? (Expose both: "tokens remaining" and "credit types" detailed).
- Accounting: do expiring E credits require revenue deferral adjustments? Need finance check.
- Edge pricing: where do embeddings fall? Map them to gmc or a distinct embedding-unit (eu) with different shelf-life semantics.
- Interop with existing starter credits and enterprise commitments. Backfill rules for old promos.

Implementation notes (prototype plan):
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): run an internal simulator on historical usage traces (sample from hosted API logs) to map expected E consumption distribution for 3 trial bundles.
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): server-side support for credit types + expiry flags + minimal UI bits in Console (balance display + expiration date).
- Phase 3 (A/B test): roll trial bundle to 5% of signups, measure activation + conversion.

Small experiments to run quickly:
- A: Give 500 mt + 3 ru, 14d expiry vs B: Give 800 mt, 14d expiry; compare 14d retention and conversion.
- C: Allow optional auto-convert 25% of E->P at checkout for 10% discount; measure uptake.

Notes to self: keep wording simple for API docs. Devs hate opaque units. Always show approximate "tokens remaining" and an equivalence calculator in Console.

References and related threads:
- see JIRA PRIC-412 for trial bundle constraints and legal note on expiring credits.
- Slack thread #pricing-ops Feb 12 2025 for suggested promo shelf-life limits.

TODOs:
- [ ] Speak with Finance (Arielle) about revenue recognition for expiring E credits.
- [ ] Run simulator with 30k sample users from Jan 2025 logs.
- [ ] Draft short Console copy that translates mt/ru->tokens for devs.

Quick sketch of Console UX copy (one-liner):
"You have 350 micro-tokens (mt) — about 5,600 tokens total — and 2 response-units (ru) for low-latency testing. Micro-tokens expire if unused for 14 days."

End of scratchpad.

Random final thought: consider a tiny negative interest on dormant E credits (slow decay) rather than hard expiry — psychologically softer but more complex to implement.
